title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations \(G=\langle x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k} | r=1\rangle\) and \(H=\langle y_{1},\ldots ,y_{\ell} | s=1\rangle\), decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
definitions: The input consists of integers \(k,\ell \ge 1\) and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.

importance.reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.

progress.text: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture show that free-group equivalence of relators cannot characterize all isomorphisms; torsion and center subclasses admit positive results.
Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain obtain strong generic rigidity and fast isomorphism algorithms for random one-relator groups.
Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups, covering one-relator groups with torsion.
Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the unrestricted one-relator isomorphism problem as open.
Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability for the separate Diophantine problem in one-relator groups.
Kapovich’s preprint extends generic small-cancellation stability and isomorphism rigidity to fixed generator and relator counts.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.

context_blocks.text: A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, \(\langle a,b | b=a^{2}\rangle\) and \(\langle x |\) empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{k}\) for the generators of G in H and \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.

sentences: Two group presentations can describe the same abstract group despite using different generators and relations.
The reviewed question asks to decide isomorphism between arbitrary finite one-relator presentations.
Candidate mutually inverse homomorphisms can be enumerated and checked using the known word algorithm.
The missing ingredient is an effective way to stop when no such isomorphism exists.
A solution would distinguish complete algebraic types within this concise presentation class, extending beyond equality and conjugacy questions about elements of one already fixed group.
